hook_text: A slope can stand for fifty years and fail in one soaked night. Here's the arm-wrestle that decides it.
clip_script: Picture every hillside as an arm-wrestle frozen in the middle. One arm is gravity, dragging every grain downhill, pushing harder the steeper the slope. The other arm is the defenders: friction, the grip of interlocked grains, and plant roots lacing the soil like the stitching in a rugby ball. While the defenders hold, nothing happens — for centuries. Mass movement is the split second the gravity arm slams the other one down. And the referee who fixes the match is water. Dip a rusk in your coffee for a second and it comes out firm — a little moisture binds. Hold it under for half a minute and it sags, lets go and drowns. Soil is the rusk. Saturate a hillside and its grains float apart, it gains tonnes of weight, and every buried surface turns slippery. Then the six movements line up like runners on a grid. Creep, the tortoise — fence posts leaning, tree trunks curving. Solifluction — cold sludge oozing over frozen ground. The landslide — a slab of hillside resigning all at once, like bricks off a tipper truck. The slump — the slide with a twist, rotating like an ice-cream scoop out of the tub. The rock fall — pure drop, straight into the steel nets. And in pole position, the mud flow — a boulder-loaded milkshake at highway speed that sets like concrete. Speed up, water up. That is why the slope that stood through fifty dry winters can fail in one soaked night.
visual_style: An arm-wrestle over a cross-sectioned hillside, a rusk dissolving in coffee in macro, then a six-lane starting grid where each lane cuts to its movement — ending on rain filling a gauge as a hillside lets go.
pacing: Steady build through the arm-wrestle and rusk, accelerating lane by lane to the mud flow, sober final beat.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn to read a hillside before the rain comes.
